speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Mr Chairman, I beg to move, "That the total sum to be allocated for Head U of the Estimates be reduced by $100".

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We are truly fortunate to have benefited from the coordinated build-up of digital infrastructure, capabilities, talent pool and smart tools through the efforts of the Smart Nation initiative.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This virtue of being prepared allows our Government agencies to respond swiftly and act decisively in our response to COVID-19.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I dread to imagine how colossal an effort it would have been to have to manually track persons on Leave of Absence and Stay-Home Notice or to contact trace hundreds of thousands, perhaps, millions of people, especially when speed is of essence to containing the spread of COVID-19.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: At the peak of the pandemic, there was so much uncertainty and Singaporeans struggled to figure out what help schemes they are eligible for and what information to believe or not to believe.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Everyone would have had a unique set of circumstances.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The sheer amount of queries received were simply overwhelming.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But, thankfully, innovations and creations such as TraceTogether, and digital tools such as the Government WhatsApp and Telegram channels, eligibility checker and chatbots, helped to achieve what we needed to, so much more effectively and efficiently.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Consequently, we were able to effectively control the spread of COVID-19 and deliver important information to Singaporeans in a very timely manner.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Could this be integrated with the SingPass mobile app, just like how we can now access our NRIC, driving licence and other useful information?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Having a robust digital capability will strongly position us for future challenges and opportunities.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Who knows when "Disease X" might strike us?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: If we are to expect vaccination e-certificates, perhaps we should consider enabling NDI for cross-border travels and transactions concurrently.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Chairman, the pandemic has threatened public health and safety, forcing individuals and organisations to cease economic and social activity and to stay within the safe confines of our homes.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: One cannot imagine how we could possibly have coped if not for the Smart Nation infrastructure that was already in place pre-COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: The Government's foresight to progressively build up our digital infrastructure and engineering capabilities have paid off handsomely.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: In the midst of a pandemic, we could count on technology to access essential services and goods, reducing exposure to the virus.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Minimising the impact of the pandemic has also allowed for our economy to enter the recovery stage, while the general population gets to resume life with some form of normalcy.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: For commercial entities, the application of smart technology pushed them to innovate and reinvent their operations or product offerings.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Not only were they able to continue their operations during the pandemic, they are even scaling new heights.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: We will continue to face multifaceted challenges, further complicated by COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Can I ask the Minister to share about how the Smart Nation will help us emerge stronger from the pandemic?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: As I mentioned earlier, we coped with this pandemic due to our resolve and helped definitely by technology.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: In the past one year, we have navigated the pandemic with the help of digital services, whether we want to find out where to collect our masks, or to see a doctor, or if it is safe to go to a mall or to a park, we would utilise the digital platforms created by GovTech.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: There are also the safe entry systems and contact tracing tools and networks which were created by the Government to help all of us stay safe.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Many of these digital services have gone a long way to directly benefit citizens and businesses.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: As we further our Smart Nation initiative, opportunities abound as well for the private sector.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: The Government has had several strategic national projects that have involved close collaboration with industry players.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: For example, the rapid development of our cashless payment system can be attributed to the hard work of our officers as well as bank service providers and merchants.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Such collaboration improves diversity of solutions and resources.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: It also contributes to job creation and makes a good training ground for budding tech experts to pilot new technologies.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: It will help our businesses to develop new capabilities and improve their product and service offerings, which will in turn stimulate economy.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Can the Minister share about how we are collaborating closer with the private sector to further our Smart Nation drive?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: There could be dire consequences if such information is wrongfully shared publicly.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: In April last year, we had two such cases.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Both incidents could have resulted in panic in the community at a time when calm was needed.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Most recently, a public servant allegedly leaked a Police lookout message that identified the suspect of the Tampines fatal stabbing incident.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The message included the suspect's name, image, date of birth and nationality.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: It was widely circulated that the man had fatally stabbed his wife.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: From that, I received calls informing me that the deceased is my ex-PCF staff, Iris.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: After her resignation from PCF, she came to bid me farewell at my Meet-the-People session.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: She noticed that I was engaging people over my exposed drink and returned with a cup cover.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: She was a good mother and brought her children well.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Her three children lost both their parents on the eve of Chinese New Year reunion dinner.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: It was a difficult period, made more difficult with the exposure.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: What role does the Government play in building digital infrastructure to support our economy and society?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Our Government has always advocated for a Smart Nation approach in building Singapore's future.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As the next generation of technology evolves and influence positive changes to our lives, there will soon be more urgent need for digital infrastructures, such as the upcoming 5G network.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: With that in mind, what is the current status of the 5G roll-out?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Are there any data security concerns and safeguards that we should take note of before we widespread adoptions?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Lastly, in which areas will the digital infrastructures enhance our governmental services online in order to better serve businesses and our Singaporeans?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: At the launch, Prime Minister Lee outlined Singapore vision to be a Smart Nation.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In the last year, we have seen how COVID-19 has accelerated the adoption of digital, affecting many aspects of our work and life, changing how we work, live and play.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Digital solutions enable new capabilities, allowing us to reimagine the way things are done.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And in doing so, how we have and how are we continuing to ensure that no one is left behind in our drive to being a Smart Nation?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In my Budget debate speech earlier this week, I did give the example of my resident struggling to get a simple task as the process had been digitalised.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And I had shared that it was not an aversion.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: How can we make it such that we make technology disappear?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Mr Chairman, in the Smart Nation Summit on 26 June 2019, Prime Minister Lee mentioned, for us, being a Smart Nation, it is not about flaunting fizzy technology, but it is about applying technology to solve real-world problems that will make a difference to people's lives.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Moving ahead, what are the Smart Nation initiatives can we look forward to to help deliver more personalised and inclusive services for our citizens?

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: COVID-19 has been a real stress test of the work that Smart Nation has embarked on for the past, more than almost seven years.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: It has exposed gaps, it has validated our investments over the many years and it has also allowed us to differentiate ourselves and to emerge stronger in a post-COVID world.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: So, the questions my team and I have asked ourselves in the last one year are the following: have our digital systems helped to save lives, enhance resilience, improve the quality of services provided to our people?

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Has it enabled us to overcome challenges collectively without leaving anyone behind?

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The digital systems that we have been building up have actually showed to be absolutely critical in our fight against COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Many of the solutions that we deployed during the crisis were developed by our in-house engineers within GovTech and other public agencies in weeks, sometimes overnight, over days.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And those of you who participated in this would know that this really helped turbo charged the delivery of these.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We had websites, MaskGoWhere, SupportGoWhere, FluGoWhere and we have the Gov.sg WhatsApp and Telegram channels.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Again, rolled out overnight and the ability to provide crucial accurate information from trusted sources enabled us as a population to respond in a coordinated, effective and calm manner.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Over 700,000 manpower and workplace applications for businesses have been made through the GoBusiness portal and that also provides convenient, comprehensive information, especially on safe management guidelines over the past year.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The Government was therefore able to continue serving people, providing services online even during the circuit breaker and thereby cushioned the social and economic impact.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Technology will be critical as we try this year to resume our daily lives.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: For instance, using the National Appointment System for COVID-19 Vaccination, eligible persons can book their vaccinations online when it is their turn.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: It is about matching supply and demand in time and space.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And for those of you who have been vaccinated, you can check your records which are available on HealthHub.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: MOH and GovTech are also developing a globally inter-operable HealthCerts standard based on blockchain technology to facilitate cross-border verification of health documents.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: There will be notarised Pre-Departure Test (PDT) test results which will be available on SingPass Mobile and we will look into extending this to vaccine certificates as suggested by Ms Tin Pei Ling.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This is actually one of the highest rates in the world.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: These achievements have only been possible because of our relentless recruitment of talent and especially in-house engineering capabilities before the crisis hit.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And we must now double down on building up our people, building up our capabilities and our agility and to use the latest cutting-edge technologies.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: One area which we will do more of is to make greater use of the cloud in order to scale new services and to re-engineer existing services.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This shift to the cloud incidentally will also make us greener and more sustainable.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We will continue to attract and nurture top ICT talent within the public sector, through our Smart Nation Scholarships, Technology Associate Programme (TAP) and other talent development programmes.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And we are not just looking for hardcore engineers but also multi-disciplinary teams – designers, analysts, policymakers, artists, communicators, in order to create really functional teams fit for purpose.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We will be launching the Digital Academy next quarter, to build up the digital skills within the wider Public Service in areas including data analytics and cybersecurity.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The Digital Academy will train more than 6,000 Public Service officers.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We hope to offer about 95 training programmes within the first year.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And I will also put in a request for Members of Parliament, those of you who want to attend these courses, please email me, and I might even try to persuade the Prime Minister to do an introductory course on C.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I have not asked the Prime Minister yet.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I share Miss Cheng Li Hui’s concern that it is critical for our public officers to carefully handle classified information in order to maintain public trust.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: All officers will undergo an annual data security programme, so that they know their responsibilities and how to safeguard the data that they handle in the daily course of activities and we will also remind our officers of the severe consequences of mishandling data.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I agree with Ms Hany Soh that the Government plays a critical role not only in shaping the national digital infrastructure but also the processes and the thinking and the mindset around it.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Just like physical infrastructure, we must commit to ensuring that our digital infrastructure, in both the hard and software side of it, is top-notch globally.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The question on 5G rollout will be handled by MCI later.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But even in that area, we will make sure that we are at the leading edge of the world and, both in terms of security and efficacy, we will be there.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The number of users of SingPass Mobile has grown.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I agree with Mr Sharael Taha that the Government's digital services must be secure, must be inclusive and must be personalised.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We have introduced the SingPass two-factor authentication (2FA) modes to ensure that SingPass remains not only secure but accessible and especially to the elderly and vulnerable groups, especially those without mobile phones.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And these include the latest use of Face Verification so that people can use Face Verification as a second factor and this will be based on matching their images against a verified database held by ICA.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Individuals can also opt to have their SMS one-time password sent to a trusted family member so that they can still have the benefit of security and the help of a trusted family member.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We are consolidating information and services for our citizens under the one-stop LifeSG app.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: If you have not used it, please go and check it out.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Users can also view the Government benefits and support relevant to them, such as GST Vouchers, Pioneer and Merdeka Generation MediSave top-ups and, soon, including the benefits that have been announced under this current Budget.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We are also improving our digital services for improved productivity and, next quarter, GoBusiness will launch an e-Service Navigator to provide our businesses easy access to over 300 Government e-services.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But more importantly, this is also an opportunity to re-engineer our processes and make Government services more suitable and facilitatory to all our businesses.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We have harnessed digital technology also to create more energy-efficient and water-efficient homes, and you will be aware of some further announcements on smart meters in both energy and water.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Mr Alex Yam has emphasised that partnership is key, and the Government and financial sector are, indeed, in fact, a very good example where this partnership has borne fruit.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Today, we have than 2.7 million users, and PayNow transactions have more than doubled in this one year.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: No doubt accelerated by COVID-19 and the aversion to handling cash.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Another example is the Singapore Financial Data Exchange which has enabled us, as individuals, to retrieve a consolidated view of all our personal finances, using either the MyMoneySense portal or a mobile banking app.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Actually, if you have not checked this out, it is a big deal because it allows data sharing which has historically been very difficult to achieve because you get a direct overview of all your financial statements and bank accounts.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But you can imagine the security needed to enable that to happen.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And this was enabled because we have central digital infrastructure riding on SingPass and MyInfo and the relationship the Government has had with the banks and our role as a neutral, trusted party to enable this kind of sharing and this kind of utility to occur.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I want to also thank the 150 Smart Nation Ambassadors who, even in the midst of the difficulties last year, volunteered to help promote the use of digital technologies, including TraceTogether.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Later this year, we will be convening a citizens panel to explore how we can improve the design of our digital services.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: So, let me conclude, COVID-19 did not change history but it has accelerated both the need and the opportunities arising from the digital revolution.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Our Smart Nation Initiative has put us in a good position to seize the moment and to prove that we can and do solve real-world problems quickly and to differentiate ourselves in the post-COVID world.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Mr Chairman, COVID-19 has provided the impetus for many Singaporeans and businesses to adopt the use of e-payments.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: E-payments make real-time payments between individuals; consumers and business; or business-to-business convenient, seamless and fast.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: It takes away the need and the risk of carrying and handling cash, saving time and effort, and is safer.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: There are clear benefits of using e-payment and we have been helping our residents as well as businesses in using and adopting e-payments.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: But we do still receive requests and feedback to ensure that e-payment does not become the only mode of payment, Because there are segments amongst our residents and even small businesses that prefer to continue to use physical cash.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: A case in point is that, during COVID, the bank branch in our constituency was closed.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: You would not believe the number of emails and requests I had to talk to the bank just to get the bank to open and there were long queues.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: I was sent photographs of long queues at other bank branches near our constituency that residents needed to go to.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Mr Chairperson, there has been a concerted effort to educate and encourage all seniors to go digital.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While such projects, like Seniors Go Digital and Hawkers Go Digital, are highly commendable, there must be the awareness of the gap between the availability of technology and the people using it.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Contactless payments through credit and debit cards have recently become the norm in Singapore, at retail merchant outlets and even in buses and trains since 2019.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Until recently, NETS relies on a PIN for verification since its inception in 1985.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Recently, though, NETS has pushed out their new contactless card with similar operating principles for contactless cards as international scheme debit cards.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This has led to some worries among the elderly.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While contactless payment has made payments easy, senior citizens are more vulnerable to scams.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The spike in bank account debit and credit-card scams in recent years has also made the elderly concerned over losing their hard-earned money in these scams.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: One of my elderly residents was told by DBS that all new cards will be contactless and they will not allow any card requiring PIN for all transactions.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: He contrasted DBS' services with OCBC's which, he said, provided a debit card which is digitally rendered non-operative by default unless so activated by the customer.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I understand that Singapore uses a chip and signature system in verifying payments through debit and credit payments.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Many European countries, on the other hand, have implemented a chip-and-PIN authentication system.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Such a system may be a good guard against attempts at fraudulent payment scams targeted at debit and credit cards.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Indeed, we have seen an increase of such cases in the recent one to two years, and many against our senior citizens.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Such cards can provide an added layer of defence to senior citizens against any fraud or scams.

speaker: The Chairman
text: The last I checked, I am still a Chairman.

speaker: The Chairman
text: So, please feel free to use that term.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Chairman, Sir, it has been heart-wrenching for us in this House to see our residents being scammed of their hard-earned monies.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Many are elderly and have little avenue to earn money lost.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As Singapore moves towards widespread adoption of digital payments, the risks are heightened.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As the money scammed are usually transferred from bank accounts, what role should banks play in trying to minimise the risks for vulnerable customers?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This will mandate the types of information financial institutions must use to verify the identity of an individual for non face-to-face contact.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I wish to follow up on a suggestion made by the former Member of Parliament for Hougang, Mr Png Eng Huat, during last year's Committee of Supply of offering an option of a cooling-off period for inter-bank transfers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On vulnerable customers, there was a Business Times article last weekend by David Hardoon, a former special adviser to the MAS.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: He noted that some financial institutions were using AI and psychometrics to help predict which customers might be more susceptible to scam attacks.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This would assist in developing bespoke advisories and training programmes to help inoculate such customers from falling prey to scams.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To what extent is the MAS working with banks on this?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In response to my Parliamentary Question in January 2021, the Minister for Home Affairs said that where the suspect was not arrested, a Court order was needed to return the money to victims, which process might take at least a year.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As such a delay could cause serious hardships, could the agencies and banks work on a more expedited process?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Mr Chairman, being an international financial centre, Singapore-based banks must remain vigilant in the fight against fraud and money laundering.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In the recent past, there had been an exponential increase in dollar value of white-collar crime that has impacted on the banking system.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In the commodities trade sector, Singapore has been rocked by trade financing fraud that has led to multi-billion dollar exposures to banks.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Some banks have withdrawn services from this sector totally.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Traders with legitimate businesses suffered a hit as it would be more difficult for them to get credit lines.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In a response dated 5 October 2020 to my Parliamentary Question, the hon Senior Minister stated that the fraud cases have been attributed to weak disclosure practices and internal controls on the part of the companies.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: What is concerning though is that, despite these weaknesses, banks have extended credit lines to such companies.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: On the part of the banks, there should have been more robust credit risk assessment of the companies.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There should be more checks, apart from just relying on paper-based processes, as they are more susceptible to the risk of fraud.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The impact of the banks’ lack of diligence is not just felt by the banks in question but the entire eco-system.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Banks regulated by MAS play a key role in preserving the integrity of our financial system.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They are, in fact, required to guard against the use of their operations to facilitate any illegitimate activity, including fraud and money laundering.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Failure to do so can have a serious impact on businesses and affect Singapore’s reputation as a premier international financial centre.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: How will MAS ensure that banks will take their responsibilities seriously in preventing fraud and anti-money laundering, especially in the context of fraud amounting to billions of dollars?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Even as Singapore grows in strength and stature as a financial centre, we need to make sure that our growth is rooted in a strong enforcement regime where all stakeholders are held firmly to their regulatory duties.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Residents in such cases may have no choice but to terminate their policies or sell them to third parties.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: It would be good if MAS could consider ways to help citizens who have to sell their policies to third parties to get a fairer value, especially under such challenging times, through better price discovery from the secondary market that is currently unregulated.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Mr Chairman, I have spoken on the value of gender diversity in the workplace and the value of a diversified board.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Climate change is a global emergency, requiring efforts from all companies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How they invest and conduct their business is a powerful lever in supporting Singapore’s Green Plan 2030.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Can the Ministry consider mandating gender diversity and green investment board disclosure for listed companies?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This can allow investors to shape their investment towards our gender diversity and sustainability aims.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We can go further by companies report on their green investment and footprint.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For gender diversity, we can look at efforts by the Board to diversify itself.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Can the Ministry also support a corporate-led movement similar to Bloomberg’s Gender-Equality Index?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It tracks the performance of companies committed to disclosing their efforts to support gender equality.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It presents a range of internationally accepted standards which companies are encouraged to choose and follow, but are not mandatory.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This has resulted in inconsistencies in reporting methods, quality in data disclosure and, hence, rendering the reports ineffective due to lack of comparability amongst the listed companies.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: According to an NUS study done in 2019 on sustainability reporting, there are clear differences in the sustainability reporting performance among different industries.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Studies are needed to determine the best frameworks to align with, such as GRI, TCFD, SASB, and so on, and we could also add industry-specific frameworks, such as RSPO.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But more broadly, can MAS share its plans to improve SGX's sustainability reporting policy to ensure quality and comparability of sustainability reports and provide support for SMEs to encourage sustainability reporting?

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Mr Chairman, on behalf of Senior Minister and Minister-in-charge of MAS, Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I will then talk about two important medium term developments for the sector asked by Members.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: One is e-payments and, two, is promoting greater social good, such as sustainable development.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: First, it is absolutely important for us to preserve and enhance the trust in our financial system.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Ms Sylvia Lim asked if banks can work with the Police for more expeditious return of monies belonging to victims of scams.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is, indeed, a concern, especially when scam cases are on an uptrend.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The banks have various measures to protect consumers.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There are various caps, daily transaction limits, ATM withdrawal limits, contactless payment limits.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Ms Sylvia Lim asked whether there could be a cooling-off period, but it is really not so practical.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The cooling-off period applies more in circumstances where you buy something and you find that it was an impulsive buy, you return it and you get your refund.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But for day-to-day transactions, I think there are serious practical limits to impose a cooling-off limit.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But I think the most important safeguard is to practise good cyber hygiene and take personal precautions.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, for consumers, this means updating security patches and anti-virus software on your electronic devices promptly; and never giving away online banking login credentials, whether it is your user IDs, OTPs and PINs, to anyone.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This includes not responding to seemingly legitimate requests for your personal and banking information, whether via email or SMS.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: No matter how genuine they look, never give that away.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Anti-Scam Taskforce under the Association of Banks in Singapore (ABS) has a specific workstream focusing on educating the public against scams.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Anti-Scam Centre under the Police, works closely with banks to freeze the bank accounts of recipients of scam monies to enable police investigations.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: However, once prosecution commences, it will be the Courts that decide when the seized monies can be returned, depending on factors, such as whether seized monies remain relevant for the purposes of investigation or trial.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: MAS understands and shares Ms Lim’s concern, and this is something we will have to consult the Police to see what is possible.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked about fraud prevention and anti-money laundering efforts in the commodities trading sector.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: MAS is working closely with other Government agencies on this.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This includes strengthening banks’ credit risk assessment on firms in the sector, and digitalising trade financing to reduce fraud risk.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: ABS, with the support of various Government agencies, has issued a code of best practices to enhance commodity financing standards in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It covers the trading companies’ corporate governance, risk management and disclosure practices.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Banks will use it to set standards for lending and this will be fully implemented by July this year.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: MAS is also working with ABS to establish a secure central database for banks to access records of trade finance transactions in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This will enhance transparency of transactions and mitigate the risk of duplicate financing.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Mr Derrick Goh asked about surrendering of insurance plans and secondary trading of insurance policies.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is partly due to the industry’s COVID-19 relief measures, which allow customers to defer paying for premium up to six months.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The applications for premium deferment have since fallen sharply by 80% between Q2 and Q4 of 2020.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We should note not all policies surrendered are due to financial hardship.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Some policyholders choose to terminate their policies because they no longer serve their needs.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Whatever the case may be, it will benefit policyholders to be able to sell the policy in secondary market, which typically fetches a higher value.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Ms Jessica Tan has asked for an update and expressed some concerns.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, let me state at the outset we cannot be dogmatic about this.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We are promoting e-payments because it is efficient, convenient and green, but we are not aiming to be a cashless society.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Cash will continue to be a familiar and convenient way to transact, as Ms Jessica Tan has experienced.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The adoption of e-payments by Singaporeans has been steadily increasing in recent years.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The COVID-19 pandemic and the rise of e-commerce have accelerated this trend.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Registrations for PayNow Corporate doubled last year to around 240,000 business users.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We expect this growth to continue, as users can now also send and receive PayNow transfers via non-bank e-wallets, such as GrabPay and Singtel Dash.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Adoption of QR payments by merchants has also surged.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There are 200,000 SGQR labels islandwide, with 120,000 deployed in 2020 alone.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And as more people switch from cash to e-payments for their day-to-day transactions, the usage of cheques has fallen.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The absolute number of cheques used fell by a record 10 million in 2020.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: These ratios should decline further as more people get used to accepting e-payments.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And there are Singaporeans who are less familiar or face difficulties with e-payments and we will not leave them behind.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The “Seniors Go Digital” initiative – Members are familiar – helps seniors acquire skills to transact digitally.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Seniors can receive personal lessons at SG Digital Offices around the island and they will be handheld, people will guide them, and I believe MOE is still pressing ahead to equip every child with a bank account and digitally-enabled bank account.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Furthermore, it is important that cash continue to be widely accepted in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There will continue to be ATMs and cash withdrawal points across our island.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As for PIN-only bank cards requested by Mr Dennis Tan, the local banks do offer customers the ability to disable the contactless feature of their ATM and debit cards, or the option of ATM cards without the contactless feature at all.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We are not aware of any bank's initiative to do away with PIN numbers.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We will remind the banks to explain this option to customers who may need it.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Another significant development in the financial services sector is the evolution of its role in promoting the larger social good.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In this regard, Mr Desmond Choo and Mr Leon Perera asked about disclosures and sustainability reporting.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We share the Members’ desire to see companies providing high-quality reports on their efforts to promote sustainability and in social contribution.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We also want to see continued improvements in how our companies disclose their broader social and environmental impact, on top of their financial performance.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Such disclosures are important, especially given the heightened social and environmental consciousness amongst investors.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It will facilitate capital flows towards investments more aligned to the investors’ preferences, objectives and standards.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: These include information, such as greenhouse gas emissions, skills and gender diversity of senior management and their board members.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In addition, the Code of Corporate Governance requires listed companies to disclose their board diversity policies, one aspect of which is gender diversity, and the progress in implementing the policies.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For financial institutions, MAS has set out its expectations with respect to the governance, management and disclosure of environmental risks.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: These disclosures are in accordance with international reporting frameworks, such as recommendations by the Financial Stability Board’s Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD).

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Notwithstanding that, in certain areas – and as pointed out by Mr Leon Perera – such as in the area of environmental sustainability, current corporate disclosures are still not where they need to be, because international standards are still evolving.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The basic problem is that there are various sustainability disclosure standards globally.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, this reduces the reliability, consistency and comparability of ESG disclosures across jurisdictions and even sectors.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: That undermines the purpose of the disclosures, which is to facilitate capital allocation decisions across competing investments.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: MAS and SGX RegCo are, therefore, carefully studying international initiatives on harmonising sustainability disclosure standards.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: One major initiative happening is that significant international standard setters are now coming together to develop unified global standards and we will monitor the developments closely.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In the meantime, MAS and SGX RegCo will continue to work with the Singapore Institute of Directors to help boards raise their sustainability reporting standards.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Mr Chairman, to conclude, let me say this.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As an international financial services centre, Singapore can contribute to the global climate change movement by mobilising capital towards low greenhouse gas emission solutions and climate-resilient development.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: These can be investments in renewable energy generation, battery technology, carbon-efficient and food production methods, so on and so forth.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The ability to achieve this and not disclosures alone, is what will move the needle and make a significant impact that is beyond Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Some observers have noted that in the recently announced Green Plan, not all the initiatives and targets are new.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is a fair and accurate observation and, in fact, it is only right that the Green Plan comprises existing as well as new initiatives.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Because, as a nation, we have been implementing strategies to preserve our environment and combat climate change for many years.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: What the Green Plan does is to try to consolidate and synergise all that we are doing, all that we are planning to do, and elevate their importance.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Each initiative under the Green Plan is a major multi-year undertaking.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For MAS, our strategy is to develop Singapore into a leading centre for Green Finance and that was announced in November 2019.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The work is cut out for MAS and the financial services sector.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 6.35 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 6.17 pm until 6.35 pm.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: However, this has not arrested the declining Total Fertility Rate, or TFR.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: The low TFR is not a situation unique to Singapore alone.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: For example, South Korea’s TFR fell to 0.92 in 2019.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: This is likely due to changing social norms and values, as many continue to prioritise their careers over marriage and parenthood.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: In the Parenthood survey that I mentioned in my Budget debate speech, there was question: "What would encourage you to have more children?" Some answered “Nothing”, “I want my life back”, “Enough”, "My parents are getting too old to help." Others said, "Trusted care-givers such as grandparents", "infant care near home and work", "I must have time for each child." But it would seem the Government have a tough job encouraging some couples to have more children.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: Given the on-going COVID-19 situation, Singapore’s TFR may dip in the near term.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: As young couples may choose to defer their marriages due to safe distancing capacity limits imposed on weddings.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: Uncertain economic conditions may also cause couples to postpone their child-bearing plans.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: Overall, this would impact our immediate marriages and fertility outcomes.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: Hence, I would like ask the Minister for an update on the impact of COVID-19 on our marriage and TFR numbers.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: I would also like to ask the Minister on whether the Government plans to review its existing strategies to encourage more Singaporeans to marry and have children, especially given changing life priorities and societal values.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But the developed countries all over the world struggle with low birth rates.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: A case in point is South Korea which has TFR lower than Singapore.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: However, South Korea still has a very lacklustre track record in terms of TFR, mainly due to the lack of desire to marry amongst the young people and also, their decision for alternate lifestyle choices.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It is obvious external outside-in strategies such as cash incentives are insufficient and they would have to be balanced with a strong dose of inside-out effort to shift social mindsets.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I seek the consideration of Government to the following suggestions to both increase TFR and our resident Singapore population.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: One, to encourage earlier marriage, consider offering support and grants to organisations with larger staff sizes and especially gender-dominant sectors like nursing, teaching, the army, to create opportunities, dignified, respectable opportunities for interaction; for example, in sports, in learning, or in forming interest clubs.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Second, also to encourage parenthood for those who are married, consider the following measures.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: For couples are willing and able to conceive, introduce even more generous housing priority benefits.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Consider second timers, for example, for HDB flat priorities and also assure couples and all of this Interim Rental Flat that they will need before they get their flat.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And for couples who are able to conceive but are reluctant or unwilling, provide respective and effective platforms for more inside-out education and sharing – dare I say, counselling – services for them to consider parenthood.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And next, on the immigration policy of Singapore, through better supporting transnational families with one Singapore Citizen parent.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Qin Hao, the stepson of my resident, came to Singapore only in his teens when his mother remarried here.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: He cannot speak very good English, but a really good boy.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: He tried very hard to catch up with his English proficiency and worked very hard in school and later went to ITE.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I helped support part of his ITE education but alas, when he reached 21 years of age, he had to leave Singapore.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: His mother, brother and stepfather are all Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In other families, foreign women either widowed or abandoned by their Singapore spouses with children, are not assured of their stay in Singapore when they apply for PR or Singapore Citizenship, due to our strict migration policies.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: They have either a mix of children born locally and/or children from their past marriages.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I seek Government’s careful consideration to include them and their children as resident Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The burden and stress they have to pay, sometimes in the form of very high school fees and healthcare costs, should be relieved.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I propose that there be more flexibility and leniency in granting both PR and citizenship to families such as them.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: Chairman, I would like to explore whether it is possible to provide more support to first-time parents, not just the financial support but also what else we can do to relieve their stress and feelings of helplessness during pregnancy and after the birth of their first-born.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: In particular, can we explore an initiative to develop a milestone booklet, akin to a baby's health booklet, to be provided to expecting couples, to track expectant mommies' well-being and to share useful information useful information by health practitioners regarding the necessary preparations for each stage of pregnancy, the parenting best practices and a list of supports systems available to all parents for the first few years of their journey into parenthood.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: There is a similar concept found in Taiwan where it is called the "Maternal Health Handbook", 孕妇健康手册, which tracks the expecting mothers physical and emotional development.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: Some examples of what I envision could be in our Singapore's version would include items such as a checklist of vaccinations required for expecting mothers, recommended dates to sign up for prenatal classes, a checklist of items to prepare for the arrival of the baby, along with tips on how to spot signs of labour or postnatal depression symptoms and where to seek support in this regard.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We have tackled this from a financial angle by various schemes to lower the cost of having children.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, in addition to financial constraints, time and stress are common concerns I hear from parents, especially those thinking about having a second child.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While some of us have the luxury of working from home, COVID-19 has also shown us the limits of this for certain groups of essential workers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For them, childcare sick leave is critical for juggling the demands of work and parenthood.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It has been more than a decade since childcare leave provisions were increased.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Public Service already gives officers childcare sick leave and it is on a per child basis.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If the Government feels that childcare sick leave is important for the people who work for us, then why is it not important for the people we serve?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Mr Chairman, in January this year, fellow Member of Parliament Mr Louis Ng raised an Adjournment Motion on “Providing more help for those undergoing IVF”.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Yesterday, Member Miss Cheng Li Hui also spoke about Assistive Reproduction Technology (ART) and fertility health yesterday.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I too relate with the topic because of residents who have shared with me their struggles.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This means that more couples are getting married at a later stage of their life.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With economic uncertainties due to the COVID-19 pandemic, like Miss Cheng Li Hui, I will not be surprised that some couples may decide to delay their marriage and may unknowingly be set back by fertility issues when they plan to have children later at an older age.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Yet, as recent as last week, I still have a discouraged couple who shared with me their emotional and financial concerns after numerous failed attempts in ART.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Given that the Total Fertility Rate has remained low and may worsen due to the pandemic and economic downturn, I would like to ask what other strategies the Government will consider to help young people understand more about fertility health earlier in their life, to better make their marriage and child-bearing plans.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Chairman, Sir, I shall not belabour the point about Singapore's dismal Total Fertility Rate (TFR).

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: What I do wish to emphasise is the reasons why we do not have enough babies and propose some measures to help bring the numbers up.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Number one, unequal care load between the men and women.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Singaporean women struggle to juggle work and care in a large part due to the lack of men's involvement in parenting.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: And fathers that I have spoken to express a spectrum of challenges, ranging from, "I don’t feel that I add much value at home because the baby only wants mommy" or "If I take leave, I will have a pile-up of work.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: It is even more stressful" or "I still need to bring the bread home." This is consistent with studies that NPTD has done, which brings us to major factor two – high work stress, no time and energy due to demands at work, make couples decide on having less children than what they would like to.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: And such resistance to taking paternity leave, made worse by workplace demands makes it necessary for stronger Government measures.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Currently, mothers receive four months of maternity leave, two months of which are subsidised by the Government.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: And this has the unintended impact of discriminatory hiring by companies who hesitate to hire women especially those who are newly married, for fear of having to bear the financial and operational costs of paid maternity leave for four months.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: This will have an equalising effect on hiring and firms will find it easier to manage the absence of a staff for two months instead of four.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Of course, we need to provide infant care courses for dads as it will be helpful to help fathers step up better and also set mothers' minds at ease.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: With such measures, we can create in time a norm in societal expectation for fathers to be present and involved in the first months of an infant's life, and subsequently as the child grows.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Studies have shown that fathers who have a close relationship with their children contribute to their sons growing up with an increased inclination to be involved dads themselves.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: If we want to cultivate a more positive mindset towards marriage and parenthood in our future generations, we need to ensure equal sharing of the load of care.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: And the time is now for us to set a new norm.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Mr Chairman, a Straits Times article in December last year provided a snapshot into the state of corruption in Singapore today.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: One of the opening lines was, and I quote, "Many people are heedless of the corruption that exists in squeaky clean Singapore, but graft remains prevalent." Over the last three to four years, the number of high profile corruption revelations have come to light.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In 2018, two Chinese Nationals, both of whom were forklift drivers were charged for collecting multiple bribes of $1 in exchange for not delaying the loading and unloading of vehicles.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Both drivers were fined and jailed between two to four months.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Corruption committed by Singaporeans and Singapore corporate entities are not condoned anywhere in the world.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Yet, the remark of graft remaining prevalent in our paper of record, no less, is a matter of concern.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While the Government is busy determining how best to reset the economy and put Singapore ahead of the pack when the post COVID-19 recovery begins, the core Singaporean value of a no-nonsense attitude towards corruption needs to be restated more forcefully.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: At stake is the reputation of the Singapore brand in a world where competition is stiffening and strong sustained growth harder to come by for a mature economy like ours.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The goodwill and confidence generated for high quality investments by a strong emphasis against corruption through the Singapore brand cannot be understated.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: CPIB be cannot afford for Singaporeans to be heedless of the corruption that exists in the country and double down on public education of its work.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In the Minister for Law's Parliamentary speech last November, the Minister spoke of the zeitgeist that is being felt worldwide with many societies grappling with debates about inequality and the sense that the elites are bending the rules and systems to their own advantage and that the structures are unfair.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Keppel Offshore and Marine or KOM scandal come to mind as does the CAD raid of S-League clubs and the Football Association of Singapore, which saw the arrest of our former Member of Parliament allegedly involved in $0.5 million donation to the ASEAN Football Federation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I understand that investigations can take some time to complete but in view of the profile of the latter two cases in particular which involve people have some status, there is a real public interest as to why these matters have not closed yet.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In the public mind, the inordinate delay in investigations is commonly juxtaposed against the publication of names, images and details of individuals splashed prominently in our papers, involving relatively petty amounts that constitute corruption like the $1 bribe, and rightly so.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To address public talk of inequality and double standards or perceptions of the same, it would be important for the CPIB and investigatory authorities to consider interim updates in view of the length of time that has elapsed since the news of the investigations broke.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In the Keppel case, many remain perplexed why the authorities are taking so long to complete investigations, especially in light of Keppel officials who have been anonymously fingered in publicly available US Department of Justice documents.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In November 2019, Keppel Offshore and Marine's lawyer who admitted to drafting contracts to make bribe payments was sentenced to a year's probation and fined $75,000 in the US.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Although a US citizen, the district judge allowed the lawyer in question to serve his probation in Singapore where he resides with his wife.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What is holding up the investigations into the Keppel matter?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Because it does not seem fathomable that the company can admit to offences but at the same time, there is insufficient evidence to lay at the feet of senior Keppel officials thus far.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Mr Chairman, Singapore has a well-known reputation of being a jurisdiction that is tough on corruption.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Singapore is the only Asian country to be ranked in the top 10.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This hard-earned reputation and result are due in no small part to our men and women in CPIB.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They deserve our gratitude for keeping corruption in check and ensuring that no one is exempted from the long arm of law even though the investigations can be difficult, arduous and may even take time.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In the 2018 Committee of Supply debate, I suggested that the main tool of the CPIB, the Prevention of Corruption Act (PCA), which was last reviewed more than 30 years ago, be updated to ensure that CPIB will continue to be able to handle the evolving challenge of corruption, in particular, cross-border corruption.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Some of the areas I suggested looking into include expanding the extraterritorial reach of PCA to include corporations incorporated in Singapore; to update the punishment provisions, especially with respect to corporations, and to consider enacting a provision similar to the UK Bribery Act; which is to make it an offence for corporations that fail to prevent the commission of bribery.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Minister in the Prime Minister's Office, in response, stated that a review was being undertaken.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: One further area which I wish to highlight for review is to statutorily provide in the PCA the attribution of company employees' corrupt actions to the company so that the company can be held liable and can be taken to task under the PCA in appropriate cases too.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As three years have passed, I will be grateful for an update of this matter.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has hit our economy very hard.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Although latest figures show some improvement in employment levels at the end of last year, we are certainly not out of the woods.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The external economic environment remains uncertain and the recovery of the labour market will take time.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In particular, the Labour Movement is concerned about the challenges faced by workers in the impacted sectors.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We are also very concerned about segments of the workforce, in particular, the mature Professionals, Managers and Executives (PMEs).

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: These employment challenges triggered by the COVID-19 pandemic accentuated what are already longer term trends and challenges facing workers, which is that technological changes are reshaping jobs, creating new jobs and also taking away the need for other jobs, which can be automated or done with fewer workers due to digitalisation.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Even without the challenge posed by COVID-19, it is challenging for workers to maintain their employability throughout a longer career span going forward.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: While workers need to be open to learn new skills, we also require employers to look ahead and identify the job changes and invest ahead in retraining, before the job changes happen.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The Public Sector is also a significant sector, which has launched its own "ITM" in the form of the Public Sector Transformation movement.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I like to ask how is the Public Service planning to ensure that its officers continue to have the pre-requisite skills and can retain their employability, as jobs are being reshaped in the transformation process?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In the same vein, how is the Public Service taking the lead in enhancing the employability of older officers?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: With the current weak labour market, is the Public Service continuing with its earlier commitment to extend retirement and re-employment ages ahead of time?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In my Budget debate speech, I highlighted how the two phenomena of work-from-anywhere and work-from-home, will result in Government having to fundamentally re-assess long-held policy beliefs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In the face of such rapid global transformation, we need to ensure that our Public Service remains agile to respond to these changes.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Our public officers will need to remain adaptable through constant upskilling and new experiences, so that they can serve Singapore effectively in the new normal.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: How will our Public Service tap on the potential of new technologies, such as artificial intelligence, 5G, and autonomous robotics?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: For our Public Service leaders of tomorrow to effectively drive transformation in Ministries and Statutory Boards, we need to ensure that we groom officers from a wide variety of background.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: While the Public Service has committed to recruit talents from both the private and people sectors, more can be done to send more officers on external attachments to acquire fresh perspectives, including to the Labour Movement.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: How many public officers have been seconded to the private and people sectors?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Can PSD set a target for key sectors, such as education, health and trade and industry?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Are our Public Service schemes ready for the day when more Singaporeans live beyond 90 years?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Lastly, as the largest employer in Singapore, companies turn to the Public Service to take the lead in adopting progressive workplace practices.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: With the new work-from-home culture, I hope that the PSD can drive the adoption of flexible working arrangements; and set the tone for companies in the private sector to follow.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Chairman, I thank Members for their views and suggestions on population matters.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We want to build a population that fosters a strong and cohesive society, sustains a strong sense of shared national identity and generates a strong, vibrant economy where all can progress, and the fruits of growth can be distributed for a fair and just society.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Singaporeans will remain front and centre of all we do.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: First, supporting marriage and parenthood remains a national priority.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Helping Singaporeans start and raise their families allows individuals to fulfil their aspirations to be a parent and also addresses an existential issue for us, which is maintaining a core of citizens born and bred here.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Miss Cheng Li Hui asked about the pandemic's impact on our marriage and fertility outcomes.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This is over and above the Baby Bonus Cash Gift.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We hope this gives some reassurance to couples to proceed with their parenthood plans.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: COVID-19 showed that flexible work arrangements (FWAs) are feasible and help parents to manage their responsibilities at work and home.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Louis Ng asked if we could introduce additional leave for parents to care for sick children.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Any leave enhancement, even if unpaid or temporary, could affect employers' operations and parents' employability, and must be reviewed with other requests for leave enhancements.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It is more difficult to introduce such changes in the current challenging economic climate.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: FWAs, on the other hand, are a pragmatic approach to meeting the needs of employers and workers.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: So, that is something that we can look at.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I agree that we need to lock in the gains of FWAs since the vast majority of employers now offer it.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We are studying the effects of increased use of FWAs and how to keep such practices.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Meanwhile, we urge employers to continue to offer FWAs to achieve better work-life harmony while at the same time, meeting business needs.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Ms Denise Phua suggested many ways to improve our Total Fertility Rate (TFR).

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Our TFR has been below replacement level for years.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We are in a similar predicament as East Asian societies like South Korea and Taiwan, and Scandinavian countries known for achieving good fertility outcomes, like Finland and Norway.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: They also experienced a drop in TFR, and some are at historic lows too.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Raising fertility is an uphill task for advanced societies, but we must continue to support those who wish to marry and have children.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Most young Singaporeans still desire to marry and have children.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The recent World Values Survey showed that families are important to Singaporeans and most want to have children – preferably two.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This is consistent with findings from the latest National Population and Talent Division's Marriage and Parenthood Survey, where over 80% of single respondents aged 21 to 35 said they wanted to get married, and 92% of married respondents in the same age group wanted at least two children.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In the last five years, or 2016-2020, the average number of citizen births also increased compared to the previous five-year period of 2011-2015.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We hope that notwithstanding the pandemic, Singaporeans will continue to pursue their family goals, and we will galvanise a whole-of-nation effort to support them.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Responding to Ms Denise Phua's suggestions, we are committed to building a Singapore that is made for families.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In the past two years, we have significantly enhanced access to affordable housing and pre-school.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We also increased the Additional Subsidy for pre-schools and raised the qualifying household income ceiling to $12,000 a month.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We aim to further lower fee caps at Government-supported pre-schools so that working families with a child in full-day childcare pay around the equivalent of fees for Primary school plus after-school student care.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: With means-tested pre-school subsidies, low- and middle-income households will pay even less.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Ms Indranee Rajah)
